speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to inform the house that the ninth session of the contracting parties to the general agreement on tariffs and trade is being brought to an end in Geneva. The session, which began last October, has been a long and important one. Naturally, since the discussions are confidential, it has not been possible to inform hon. members of what has been going on. However, I know that members of the house have a strong interest in the GATT and will want to know what has happened as soon as possible.
This ninth session really had two purposes. In the first place, it covered the normal routine business for which the members of the GATT assemble approximately every six months. In addition, however, at the suggestion of quite a large number of the contracting parties, there was a review of the articles of agreement, and consideration of the constitution of a new organization to administer the agreement. By far the greater part of the work of the session was related to these matters.
In addition, the firm binding of the tariff schedules under the agreement comes to an end on June 30 of this year, and recommendations have been made to governments tor the future of tariff schedules. This is one of the matters about which I shall make a full explanation at a later date.
Accordingly, this ninth session has covered a wide range of subjects. This includes the
tariff schedules to which I have just referred. It has also included a review of the basic rules of trade and of the various escape clauses. These escapes include those provided for countries in balance of payments difficulties and also those provided for underdeveloped countries. The review has covered the provisions of the agreement for agricultural trade, and further arrangements have been made leading toward the accession of Japan to the general agreement. Finally, a good deal of attention has been paid to the possibility of putting the GATT on a rather firmer organizational basis; so far, as hon. members will recall, it has only been applied on a provisional basis.
Delegates of 35 countries are now on their way home from Geneva. When they get home they will inform and advise their governments. Some, of course, have a good deal farther to go than others, and it has been agreed that complete information regarding the ground covered in the ninth session will be delayed for two or three weeks in order to give all concerned an equal chance to digest it. At the appropriate time, and as soon as I can, I shall be making a full statement in the house. In the meantime some announcements are being made by common agreement in Geneva. I shall draw them to the attention of the house as they become available.
The information to be released in Geneva in the near future will refer chiefly to the routine items of the ninth session, rather than to the review and amendments of the articles of agreement. These items are all closely interrelated and their over-all effect can best be judged by reviewing them as a single parcel. I am sure hon. members will agree that it would be most satisfactory if I made a complete statement later on, rather than two or three piecemeal statements, even though newspaper reports will be appearing from time to time.
However, I think I should make it clear at this time that the GATT will go on. We already have an agreement which is being provisionally applied by the member governments, and this agreement will continue.
In regard to amendments that have been proposed, I have only one remark to make at this time. This is to say that while they do not add up to as strong and effective a GATT as I had hoped last October when the

Inquiries of the Ministry review began, they do add up to a more satisfactory agreement than I had feared when I returned from Geneva last December. The result is not as good as it might have been, but it might have been much worse. It will continue to be in Canada's interest to adhere to the GATT.
May I ask the minister if while we are waiting for him to make his extended statement as promised the texts of t'he agreement might be made available?

speechtext: I understand that the prepared statement will be out well ahead of the texts of the agreements. I will table the texts of the agreements as soon as they come to hand, which will be in perhaps three or four weeks.

The house resumed, from Monday, March 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. McCann:
That a select committee be appointed on broadcasting to consider the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and to review the policies and aims of the corporation and its

Special Committee on Broadcasting regulations, revenues, expenditures and development, with power to examine and inquire into the matters and things herein referred to and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and to send for persons, papers and records; that the committee have power to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be deemed advisable or necessary; that the committee have power to meet while the house is sitting; that the committee shall consist of the following members; Messrs. Balcer, Beaudry, Boisvert, Bryson, Carter, Cauchon, Decore, Diefen-baker, Dinsdale, Fleming, Gauthier (Portneuf), Gauthier (Nickel Belt), Goode, Hansell, Henry, Holowach, Kirk (Shelburne - Yarmouth - Clare), Knight, McCann, Monteith, Reinke, Richard (Ottawa East), Richardson, Robichaud, Studer, Weaver; that standing orders 64 and 65 be suspended in relation thereto.

Mr. Speaker, the last occasion on which the house engaged in a debate on matters pertaining to radio broadcasting and television was on June 4, 1954, when several of the estimates then before the committee of supply afforded a rather limited opportunity for discussion of this important subject.
Her Majesty's loyal opposition welcomes not only the resolution but the opportunity which it now affords for discussion of this subject. The resolution proposes the appointment by the house of a select committee on broadcasting to consider the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and to review the policies of the corporation and its regulations, revenues, expenditures and development.
We consider it most timely that the house should undertake such a study. Similar select committees have been appointed by the house from time to time. Looking back over recent years one recalls that similar select committees were appointed by the house in the sessions of 1942, 1943, 1944, 1946, 1947, 1950, the second session of 1951 and 1953. It is therefore two years since the last select committee was appointed to undertake this task. We have asked for the appointment of this committee and we welcome the proposal. So far as our contribution to the membership of that committee is concerned, we shall do all that lies within our power to make the committee effective for the purpose of inquiring into these aspects of the administration and policies of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and of the government in relation thereto.
In speaking today on this subject it is necessary to bear in mind the fact that the last annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation brings us down to March 31, 1954 and no further. In this debate we are therefore dealing with a report the most recent portion of which is at least 11 months old.
I propose today to have something to say on several subjects bearing upon policy and


administration. I begin with the important subject of the system under which control is exercised over radio broadcasting in Canada. This is not a new subject and what I have to say on the matter today is by no means new, but I put it forward today by way of reassertion of the position which the Progressive Conservative party has consistently taken.
We have in Canada today, in the field of radio broadcasting, the government-owned corporation, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, operating networks as well as stations which operate locally, and we have also 150 privately-owned and operated broadcasting stations. Over those 150 privately-owned broadcasting stations the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, under the authority of statute, exercises the widest powers of control and regulation. I am not at the moment speaking of the extent to which those powers have been exercised but I am drawing attention to the breadth of those powers and their sweeping nature.
It is also a fact outstanding in this relationship that these privately-owned stations and the publicly-owned stations are, to a large extent, competitive. They are competitive, at any rate, to the extent to which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, with its sweeping powers, permits those privately-owned stations to become competitive with the publicly-owned system. It is then a cardinal feature of this system as it now obtains that the publicly-owned system operated by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is not only engaged in the operation of radio stations and networks but is also holding the power and discharging the function of regulator of all radio broadcasting in Canada by some 150 privately-owned stations.
We think that this system is not sound. We think that too much power is placed in the hands of this one government agency. We urge again-as we have consistently urged -that we shall arrive at a much better system of administering control and regulation of broadcasting in Canada if we leave to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the important task of operating stations and networks in Canada and place in the hands of another public body the responsibility for exercising that control and regulation of all radio broadcasting in Canada which this parliament may consider necessary from time to time.
There are important precedents which ought to guide our thinking in this direction. I draw attention to the fact-and I think it can be summed up in a sentence-that today with respect to its competitors the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation can, if it so chooses,

exercise dictatorial power. It is at the same time judge and policeman over those of its competitors whom it permits to enjoy in their operations enough power to come into competition with it. We believe that competition is a good thing. It is a good thing for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as well as for others. We think that the best results will be obtained if competition is permitted and if those powers now wielded by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the field of control and regulation are transferred to another public body operating in the public interest. The public interest will in no wise suffer if those powers to which I have referred are placed in the hands of a different public body.
When two years ago the MacQuarrie committee brought in its report following an extensive review of the operations of the Combines Investigation Act, they arrived at the conclusion that it was undesirable that there should be concentrated in the one official the investigation and then the decision as to whether there should be prosecution. That committee expressed its views in this regard in these words. Speaking of the commissioner it said:
He is given the compromising appearance of being "at one and the same time prosecutor and judge".
And it continued further:
... as long as a single official is placed in the position of being required to perform incompatible functions there is room for a good deal of public misunderstanding.
For these reasons which commended themselves to the government as well as to the house, Mr. Speaker, the house adopted legislation to detach from the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act certain functions, leaving to him the duty to investigate and conferring on another body then created, namely the restrictive trade practices commission, the duty and responsibility of review. That is a useful precedent to guide the house in this matter.
There is also, of course, the useful and outstanding precedent that we have with respect to regulation of railway transport in Canada. The board of transport commissioners has now been in existence in this country for half a century. It exercises such regulatory functions as are conferred upon it by the Railway Act alike over the publicly-owned Canadian National Railways system and the privately-owned Canadian Pacific Railway. I venture to say that hon. members of this house would view with horror any suggestion that the regulatory and controlling functions now exercised by the board of transport commissioners over the Canadian Pacific Railway should be conferred upon the Canadian 50433-115
Special Committee on Broadcasting National Railways. Yet, Mr. Speaker, that is precisely the situation we have in Canada in this important field of communication in the form of radio broadcasting.
Again, the kind of system that we advocate has been introduced in Australia and is operating satisfactorily. There is a five-man board there exercising controlling and regulating functions over both the government-owned and privately-owned stations and networks. I emphasize that the system is working satisfactorily.
I ask hon. members of this house to face up to this question: Is it right or can it be sound policy that there should be vested in this corporation, which has important duties to discharge with respect to the operation of stations and networks, these extremely wide controlling and regulatory powers?
Le Matin, in its issue of June 11, 1954, drawing attention to this situation where the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation exercises dual functions, had this to say in an article headed:
(Translation):
A Threat to Freedom
With regard to private stations the C.B.C. is all at once policeman, competitor, lawyer, judge, jury and executioner.
(Text) :
Now, sir, is there any hon. member of the house who thinks that so many and conflicting and incompatible functions can be discharged by the one body? We of Her Majesty's loyal opposition consider that we would have a much better system if these regulatory powers were vested in a different public body. That was also the recommendation of a very distinguished member of the Massey commission, Dr. Arthur Surveyer, who-and one says this with the highest respect for all other members of that royal commission-was perhaps the man best qualified by technical experience to express his opinion in this respect. His recommendation, as found at page 391 of the report of the Massey commission, is as follows:
That the Canadian Broadcasting Act should be amended to provide for the creation of an independent regulatory body with authority and jurisdiction over the activities of both the privately and the publicly owned broadcasting and telecasting stations, this body to report to the Minister of Transport and to be known as the Canadian broadcasting and telecasting control board.
It is a board of that type that we have in mind and which we earnestly recommend to the house. It is unwise, sir, it is fundamentally unsound, that this corporation, which as I have said is competitor to a large and a wholesome extent with privately-owned stations, should be permitted to rule over them; and whether or not there is an attempt

Special Committee on Broadcasting to engender any form of fear the fact remains that as long as you have a system like that these privately-owned stations are necessarily living under some sense of fear because no licence is granted except on the recommendation of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Now, sir, we are not alone in urging an improvement of the kind I have proposed in our system. It has been recommended indeed by important Liberal organizations in this country. The young Liberals of Canada have recommended the very type of system that I am advocating today, not once but several times. They have publicly espoused proposals that an independent body should be established to license and regulate all radio and television stations in Canada.
Under section 21, subsection 1 (c), of the Canadian Broadcasting Act the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation enjoys the power to make regulations to control the character of any and all programs broadcast by the corporation or private stations. Sir, this is just too much power to place in this one body.
The situation has greatly changed in Canada since the present system was first adopted and written into our statutes. At the time that the system was established no one, I am sure, taking part in the writing of the statute foresaw that we would have in Canada today something like 150 private stations operating and giving important and valued service to the public. We must adjust the system that was adopted more than a score of years ago to changed conditions.
This proposal has not been rejected by the committees of the house that have sat in recent years. The last committee in 1953 received proposals to this effect but did not reject them. If you will look at the report of that committee presented to the house on May 9, 1953, and found at page 653 of the Journals of the house, you will find that in the twelfth paragraph of the report the committee had this to say:
Particular reference might perhaps be made to the submission of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters in view of the fact that the committee devoted some time to a discussion of the views of the association on the subject of regulation. The committee detected a more reasonable approach to this subject than in former years in that the association appeared to concede the necessity for regulation and co-ordination of broadcasting in Canada but suggested that such functions should be carried on by a "separate regulatory body". The committee was unable to study this subject with the care which it would appear to merit in the light of the continued interest which is expressed therein and which would be necessary in view of the concept of a national system with control vested in a single body responsible to parliament, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.


So far as the last committee which sat two years ago is concerned, therefore, it recognized the proposal I am now advocating as one having considerable merit justifying a more extensive inquiry and consideration than the committee of that year felt it could devote to it. It did not reject the proposal; on the contrary, it indicated that the proposal had merit.
I am not going to detain the house long in discussing the programs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I think all of us are quite happy to pay tribute in many respects to the programs that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation offers to the public. Nevertheless, sir, in recognizing that probably most of the type of programming that the corporation does is of a high order, that should not turn us aside from our duty to criticize where criticism is fair and will have salutary effects. I do not know why it is that the corporation, with all the opportunities that are open to it to conduct programs of a different type, found it necessary on the eve of Christmas to broadcast a program the effect of which is described in the following Canadian Press dispatch emanating from Winnipeg on December 24:
A C.B.C. television program Thursday night, reported to have decried the Santa Claus myth, brought tears to the eyes of some children, a Winnipeg father said today. George Stokes said in an interview he had invited eleven neighbourhood children to his home for a small Christmas party. They were watching T.V., he said, when the program, Press Conference, from Vancouver came on. Mr. Stokes said one of the three men sitting at the "discussion" table was "very haphazardly" dressed as Santa Claus. He and the other two concluded that it was time the "myth" was exposed and taken from the Christmas celebration, Mr. Stokes said. "Two of the little fellows began to cry", Mr. Stokes said. "The whole program was in very poor taste, particularly at this time". He said all the youngsters watching the program ranged from 4 to 7 years, an age when Santa Claus "means a great deal to them".
I am not going to dwell on the more lugubrious features of this report, but I wonder whether any one of us has a good word to say for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation emitting a program of that kind on Christmas eve. They have lots of other programs suitable to the season without sending out that one. It is not many years ago that we had a controversy on parliament hill over a deputy minister who undertook to explode what he regarded as a number of myths, Santa Claus being one, as well as many of the most cherished religious beliefs held by many of us, with which he was prepared to do away. I hope that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will not permit its programs to be used for similar purposes.

Then there is the question of Canadian content. I shall have something more to say on this subject shortly as applied specifically to television. I am addressing my remarks now also to sound broadcasting. It will be recalled that the minister laid emphasis on this in his statement last night. One of the guiding principles upon which the Massey commission based its report was the necessity for preserving and enlarging the Canadian content of programs. Let us recognize that the privately-owned and operated stations in Canada have done much to develop Canadian talent through the place given to such talent on their stations. Before the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or the government take more credit than is due them in this respect, I should like to quote some views attributed in the press of July 3, 1954, to the Canadian council of authors and artists. As you will see, they are far from satisfied with the extent to which the corporation is making use of Canadian talent, although the corporation is enjoying vast revenues today voted to them for that purpose and on the understanding they would be used for the development of Canadian content in their program. This is the dispatch:
The Canadian council of authors and artists expressed strong disapproval of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's program content at its annual meeting concluding in Montreal last week.
Delegates attending the conference were dismayed that during the most active production period of February through April 1954, only 14-43 per cent of the entire schedule of Toronto's CBLT station involved the services of free-lance artists represented by the council, while only 38-32 per cent of the entire schedule was made up of program material originated in Canada.
The French-speaking delegates also expressed the opinion that the Canadian content on the French outlets was "deplorably low".
On the basis of the survey, old films and imported foreign programs made up the 61-68 per cent of the schedule. Since the 15 per cent tax was declared by the C.B.C. to be for the purpose of developing a predominantly Canadian program service, the CCAA is indignant. The council suspects the danger of a similar situation in radio and hopes that the C.B.C. will originate programs with a more Canadian flavour-and more Canadian freelance artists at work in them, of course.
One of the other purposes that the Massey commission held before us was that there should be a diminution in the commercial content of all programs. It was because the corporation was at that stage dependent to a large extent upon revenues from commercial broadcasts that the commission recommended that public sources of revenue be placed at the disposal of the corporation, obviously in the hope that the commercial element in the programs offered by the corporation would be reduced. But what has been the result, sir? The result has not been a diminution in the commercial element in the 50433-1151
Special Committee on Broadcasting programs of the corporation. The corporation is deriving a much larger revenue today from commercial sources that it did when the Massey commission wrote its report. But let us be fair. Part of that increase, of course, is attributable to the fact the corporation is now engaged in the field of television. But we, as hon. members, had a right to expect there would be a substantial reduction in the commercial element of these programs, and there has not been that reduction.
In the field of talks, one immediately enters a controversial sphere. I wish to say again, as I have said on previous occasions in the select committee in other years, that the talks sponsored by the C.B.C., so far as they range over the realms of economics and politics, are in our view too much left of centre, and in the political realm those talks are much too pro-Liberal government. In this committee we shall ask for detailed statements of those who have participated in these talks and commentaries and the payments made to them. We do not propose, so far as we have the opportunity of avoiding it, to tolerate any reluctance in giving that information to the committee so the public will be able to reach a fair estimate as to whether or not those talks are properly balanced.
I shall mention one other matter before T leave the subject of programs, and it relates-to a subject that is not new. It is the subject of time given to communists. In the last-general election on the national system of the-Canadian Broadcasting Corporation free time' was given to the communists. This was done under regulations promulgated by the corporation and approved by the government. It may be that at that particular stage the corporation, in view of the number of candidates nominated for that express purpose, of course, by the communists in this country, could not deny the communists some time on the air. I believe it was the duty, and is the duty today, of the corporation and the government to amend the regulations to the extent necessary to see to it that free facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, maintained at public expense, are not put at the disposal of the communists to spew forth their filthy propaganda across this country. The government has neglected this issue for a long time. This subject has been before successive committees but no action has been taken. We are renewing our demand that action be taken.
Le Matin of Montreal in its issue of July 3, 1954, had this to say on the subject:
(Translation):
In 1944 the Liberals' kindness to the communist party went so far as to include an invitation to Tim Buck to participate in a series of talks under the general title "Speaking as a Canadian", whereas
1816	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Broadcasting it is a well known fact that neither this gentleman nor the other Marxists are entitled to speak as Canadians.
(Text):
Others have said the same thing. This is an issue that can no longer be ignored by the government.
I shall be very brief in my comments on the changes proposed in the appropriations for the international shortwave operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, as agent for the government. The estimates for the fiscal year which will commence on April 1 indicate that the appropriations for this service are to be reduced from this year's figure of $2,464,844 to a figure of $1,807,825, a reduction of 26 per cent. This will mark the first check in a steady ten-year expansion of this service, which in 1953 added Polish as the 16th language in which broadcasts are sent abroad.
The minister has indicated that no reduction is intended in the broadcasts to countries behind the iron curtain, but there will be an elimination of the present daily broadcasts to countries in western Europe, and some reduction in the broadcasts to the countries of Latin America.
We in that committee I think will wish to be very sure that the policy in this regard is closely co-ordinated with the policy being followed by the Department of External Affairs. It is evident that what the government contemplates now is that broadcasts through the international shortwave service are to be intended less for friendly countries than to be a factor in psychological cold warfare. In this respect I think we wish to know what efforts are being made to co-ordinate and to avoid duplication with other services intended for the same purposes, such as the "Voice of America," and the foreign service of the British Broadcasting Corporation.
In this regard I would like to make a specific proposal to the government, that the estimates bearing upon the international shortwave service should be referred to the select committee on broadcasting for consideration.
I now turn to the subject of television. The importance of television cannot be gainsaid by anyone. Last night the minister referred to the tremendous influence of television in this country and, to use his expression, said that it was "one of the biggest developments in the history of our country."
The Globe and Mail of Toronto of January 13 reports Mr. Dunton, chairman of the corporation, as follows:
Mr. Dunton said many Canadians who have taken the attitude that TV is not for them and will have nothing to do with it are wearing blinkers.


Television is fast becoming one of the major means by which people get their impressions, he said, and everybody should pay some attention to what is going on.
Every hon. member in this house must echo those sentiments. Television is enjoying in Canada today a veritably prodigious growth. It is a force which has implications for the home life, the social habits and the thinking of Canadians that I am sure go far beyond the estimates of any one of us in the house today.
Mention was made last night of the tremendous sale of television sets in Canada. Some more direct figures on that subject will, I think, serve more than one purpose in the light of what I propose to say later. Here is an extract from a bulletin issued by the dominion bureau of statistics on February 25:
Canadian manufacturers sold a record 623,856 television sets for $216,451,362 last year as against 366,498 for $148,753,479 in 1953. Since September 1949 sales of Canadian made TV sets have numbered 1,200,561 worth $451,332,214 at factory prices.
There you have the figures for the years 1954 and 1953, laid side by side. They show that there has been an increase of 70 per cent in the number of sets sold in 1954 over those sold in 1953. On the other hand, sir, the dominion bureau of statistics reports that for the same period there was a reduction in the number of radio receiving sets sold. This is the report:
Sales of radios by Canadian manufacturers dropped last year-
That is, 1954.
-to a post-war low of 487,237 sets worth $35,816,274 from 620,860 sets valued at $52,119,381 in 1953.
In other words, 1954 witnessed a reduction of 22 per cent as compared with 1953 in the number of radio receiving sets sold in Canada. And in the year 1954 the number of television sets outnumbered for the first time the number of radio receiving sets sold in Canada.
In the face of this tremendous expansion, and in the face of this evident widespread public interest in television, what is the policy of this government? Here we are talking about no mere regulatory policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We are talking about a policy of the government which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is required to carry out.
There was a lot of fine talk last evening about what has been accomplished. The fact remains that the development of television in Canada was delayed by deliberate government policy. For years they sterilized the development of television in Canada by a paternalistic policy.
The minister offered some figures last night, telling us that Canada is second in the area

covered by television, and second in the number of stations. Surely the minister will not compare a country like Canada with a compact country like the United Kingdom, where a small number of television stations can reach a far larger number of people in a very much smaller area. These figures are very interesting; but on analysis the comparisons in which the minister indulged last night were not very significant.
But while we are impressed by and glad to see this development in television, let us bear in mind that it is the result of a partial opening of the gates by the government, after having walled up its policies against the development of television in Canada for years.
Last night the minister found it within his generosity to pay tribute to those to whom he referred as the pioneers in the development of private telecasting stations in Canada. Well, there are a great many others who would have been quite prepared to enter this field, and to have entered it long ago if, by deliberate government policy, they had not been prevented from doing so. There were willing to be pioneers, prepared to risk their own means, but they were not Permitted to do so by the government.
And now we have still the other feature of government policies with respect to television, the policy of local monopoly. Some, no doubt-perhaps some hopeful souls-had expected that last night the minister would have made some announcement that the time had come for a change in government policy in this respect, an announcement of some departure from the rigidity and the rigours of this monopolistic policy the government has followed with respect to television in Canada. But, no, there is still no indication when the government is prepared to depart from its monopolistic policy. Sir, that policy means simply this, that the government does not intend to allow any privately-owned station to go into an area now served by one of the stations operated by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It does not matter whether they are willing to do so; it does not matter whether it is their own money they are risking; it does not matter that competition is a good thing, and would be a good thing for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
No; the government prefers to follow its general arid policy of monopoly. That policy is fraught with very grave dangers. I make no apology for quoting again in the house an extract from a speech made on May 14, 1954, by Mr. Dunton, chairman of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Speaking on that date at Saskatoon in relation to this subject of freedom
Special Committee on Broadcasting of expression and freedom of choice-and it is of the essence of freedom that there should be freedom of choice-he said this:
But conditions have changed since the early days of the original fights for freedom of expression. Now a relatively small number of great printing presses turn out a large part of the actual reading material of most people. A few transmitting stations put out all the broadcasting heard effectively by the population of a whole region. A handful of men control the making of most moving pictures seen by millions. In effect a small number of men-publishers, broadcasters, film organization heads-can control a large part of the ideas and impressions and opinions that reach the minds of most people.
I think that if we are realistic we have to admit that an inherent danger to a genuinely free and fair interchange of ideas has developed from the concentration of so much power over means of mass communication in the hands of so few. I am very conscious of this myself because I and others of the C.B.C. belong to the few, together with controllers of publishing, film and other broadcasting organizations.
And then he says further:
There is true freedom in mass communication only if ideas which happen to appeal to lesser numbers of people have a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Then people as a whole have a chance to weigh and choose, and perhaps change their minds, for themselves. The essence of freedom lies in freedom to choose from a variety of alternatives; if there are no alternatives-in kinds of ideas and material presented-there can be no freedom of choice.
Does anyone here think, if in the field of television the source of ideas and opinions expressed is confined to one telecasting source in an area, that the people in that area are going to have that freedom of choice which is so essential to the preservation of freedom and freedom of men's minds? No matter how conscientiously the program authority in that particular station may work, it is a fact that it will be more to expect than anyone with a sound knowledge of human nature would expect, that there is going to be such a variety of ideas expressed as to afford that freedom of choice which is so valuable to us all.
Competition is a good thing for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Mr. Dunton as far back as 1946 in the committee of that year admitted that competition had had a beneficial effect on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. During the proceedings of the committee I asked him, on August 2, 1946, this question, to which he gave a frank answer, as one would expect:
Do you not think that competition as best afforded by the private stations does work to the benefit of C.B.C., and so to speak, keep C.B.C. on its toes?
A. In any reasonable measure of competition between two people a certain stimulus is given to them. That is one reason the board has advocated that a number of private stations be approved. The people have a choice of programs and the element of competition enters into it.
If competition is a good thing for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the

Special Committee on Broadcasting field of sound broadcasting, why is it not a good thing for the C.B.C. in the field of television? Why should it be government policy, as it has been for years, to permit the licensing of sound broadcasting stations in areas where they are in direct competition with C.B.C. stations and yet at the same time to deny any other stations privately-owned an opportunity of entering into competition with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in any area where it is operating a television station? Surely what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. If competition was good for the C.B.C. in one case it should be good for the C.B.C. in the television field as well.
You have a pointblank contradiction here in government policy. It was brought out clearly in the 1953 committee, and at page 469 of the proceedings of that committee will be found some questions which I asked of Mr. Browne, the official of the Department of Transport who is in charge of licensing in these matters. I said to him:
You say there is no policy against licensing two or more stations in the same area?
A. There is no government policy which restricts the number of stations, of which I am aware.
Q. In other words, it is not the policy to foster a local monopoly in sound broadcasting?
A. There is no government policy, as I have said, akin to that which at the present time applies in the case of television.
It is time that the policy in television was brought into line with the policy with respect to the licensing of stations for sound broadcasting.
What I have to say in this respect about the beneficial effects of licensing private stations applies with respect to the French language as well as to the English language. Hon. members of this house were shocked on March 17, 1953, when the then minister of transport entered into the debate and said that in order to preserve the position of the French language in television it was necessary that this policy of C.B.C. monopoly in television should be preserved. How could anything be farther from the truth? French language private television stations should be licensed so that they may be brought into beneficial and effective competition with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and give the people in French-speaking areas an opportunity of having alternative sources of television.
At the very time that the minister was putting forward that proposition which was so lacking in any element of factual basis, the policy of the government was to deny an application by La Presse which was then pending for the licensing of a television station in Montreal, and to delay applications for other stations as well. Of course we


should remember that this was just before the election of 1953, and we know well that both before and during elections Liberal political morality notoriously deteriorates.
At this very time the policy in the United Kingdom, which formerly was one of monopoly in television as in sound broadcasting, has been reversed, and the new policy is to allow a number of privately-owned stations to enter the field of television.
What has been the consequence of this policy of monopoly fostered by the government? The result has been that the C.B.C. has picked off the plums of the large urban areas of Canada and has taken a dog-in-the-manger attitude that nobody else shall be permitted to enter those areas and establish stations. What has been the effect on listener interest? People in the city of Toronto have the opportunity of listening to United States programs, whether they come to them over the C.B.C. station CBLT or the stations in Buffalo. You can roam at will over the findings of listener ratings in that area from the time that CBLT, the C.B.C. television station in Toronto, came into operation right down to the present time, and you will find that initially 80 per cent and now two-thirds of the listener interest goes to the Buffalo stations.
No, no.

Yes. There has been some improvement; there has been some increase in that period in the popularity which CBLT enjoys with listeners in the Toronto area. I am speaking this afternoon not by way of condemnation of the efforts of CBLT to give interesting programs in that area, but to indicate why this policy of the government in denying an opportunity to others to have alternative sources of television programs is wrong. This is what happens when people have the opportunity. True, United States stations are available in Toronto for their selection. The government policy has denied opportunities to these people to hear other Canadian stations.
Every now and again when this question is raised the government purports to invoke the Massey commission report in support of their policy. The Massey commission report cannot be put to any such use. What the Massey commission majority report recommended in this regard, as found at page 303 of the report, is this:
That no private television broadcasting stations be licensed until the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has available national television programs and that all private stations be reauired to serve as outlets for national programs.
The government has sought to treat that as the equivalent of a recommendation that

there should be monopoly in favour of the government stations in the urban areas of Toronto, Montreal, Halifax, Winnipeg and Vancouver. However, sir, that attempt is completely exploded by a speech Mr. Massey made to the Canadian Club at Montreal on June 11, 1951, not long after the report of the royal commission was tabled in this house. This is what he said, I take it, by way of correcting the misinterpretation which had by that time been placed upon the report by the government:-
Although our report is long and involved, on only one point does there appear to be some misunderstanding. May I mention it now? My colleagues and I recommended that private television broadcasting stations be licensed only when the C.B.C. has available national programs, some of which the private stations would use. This does not mean, however, that there can be no television in. say. Vancouver, or Halifax, until the C.B.C. has completed a system of national television networks, a long and costly business. We were talking of programs. The national programs would, of course, be in the form of films or of kinescope, which for a long time to come will no doubt form a large part of the program material of television in Canada on all stations, whether private or C.B.C.. until the time when television networks in Canada are possible.
You will see from this there is nothing in the report of the Massey commission which justifies this continued policy of local monopoly.
I do not intend to comment on what the minister had to say last night concerning the establishment of television networks except to say that there was no surprise in what he had to say. His statement was accurately foreshadowed by the press report which appeared on February 25. I hope the committee will have an opportunity of inquiring fully into the proposed arrangements for the operation of television networks.
I should like to return to the subject of Canadian content in the television programs. I need not repeat what I said earlier as coming from the Canadian council of authors and artists in this regard. The reason parliament approved the establishment of the type of national system which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is operating now in television and the reason that parliament has placed at the disposal of the corporation huge sums of money in this respect was, as we were told, to maintain the Canadian nature of television broadcasting. The Massey commission report said this, at page 301:
The pressure on uncontrolled private television operators to become mere channels for American commercial material will be almost irresistible.
For that reason we were called upon to approve this national system and to make available these vast sums of money. What do we find? I have before me what I believe is a sample week taken from station CBLT
Special Committee on Broadcasting Toronto, May 30 to June 5, 1954, based upon the Elliott-Haynes survey, a very competent and reputable survey. Let us ask ourselves the question whether the purpose of providing these funds and establishing the system has been fulfilled by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation under this system approved by the government. The total number of hours covered in this week on station CBLT was 38-5. The hours of Canadian originated material were 15-5 or 40 per cent. The hours of United States originated material were 21 or 55 per cent. The hours of B.B.C. originated material were two, or 5 per cent. I have this analysis of the Canadian material. I mentioned that the total hours of Canadian originated material were 15-5. Of those hours 7-5 were devoted to news, films, remote (sport or actuality), and eight hours were devoted to live Canadian talent shows. In other words, Canadian content was to be found in 40 per cent of the time in this typical week on station CBLT and of that 40 per cent only half comprised live programs involving the use of live talent. Therefore I say the bogey that was held out that licensed private stations would be under irresistible pressure to become channels for United States programs and that the C.B.C. alone could resist that pressure has been completely exploded.
It has been shown that the C.B.C. system is permitting its programs to carry United States material for more than half the time and a relatively small portion of the programs is drawn from live Canadian talent.
As far as advertising is concerned, we know very well that in order to keep up revenues and in order to attract sponsorship for certain of these programs the C.B.C. has resorted to reduction of rates off the card rates for advertising. The taxpayer subsidizes the program.
In the city of Toronto we have witnessed the theft by the government of T.V. channels. The government will not let any private operator have any of the channels there, and they have permitted the theft of one of the channels which has now gone elsewhere. This has been done to the knowledge of all Liberal members in this house representing ridings in the city of Toronto, yet not one voice from the other side of the house has been raised in this house in protest against this theft of channels or in protest against the continued denial of licensing to private stations in that area. Apparently it is popular thinking with the hon. members opposite who come from Toronto that this policy of monopoly should be continued.
I turn now to the final subject of finances. We are witnessing today the inevitable effects of the deliberate government policy of removing from parliament the financial control

Special Committee on Broadcasting over the C.B.C. We see in the last available report of the C.B.C. that that very fortunate government agency is literally wallowing in the wealth that has come from the windfalls from tax revenues put at its disposal by the government. That kind of situation is an invitation to indulge in high expenditure and loose methods of control. It is bound to lead to inefficiency and extravagance. The government has followed a policy of spoonfeeding. It has been pumping millions of dollars into the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation much beyond the digestive capacity of that corporation. Let us look back at what happened.
In 1951 the Massey royal commission recommended that the C.B.C. should have funds voted to it by parliament rather than that it should collect the proceeds of the $2.50 nuisance tax on radio receiving sets. The government was not satisfied to propose a system of annual grants, a system which would have maintained the principle and the practice of parliamentary control. Oh, no. Too much responsibility to parliament would have been involved in any such proposal. That was not for them. So they recommended to the house-and an obedient majority in the house adopted their proposal -that for a period of five years the C.B.C. should have a grant of $6,250,000 a year. That was done. Parliament has no control over that fund. We of the official opposition recorded our emphatic opposition to that proposal because of its inherent unsoundness. We said that in each year parliament ought to deal with the needs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation after thorough review of them. Parliament is surely competent to deal with every situation on its merits; and if the C.B.C. wants to plan ahead, then surely it can trust parliament to realize and to meet its needs in that respect.
This government has a mania for removing from parliamentary control everything that it can put beyond the reach of parliament. So they went a step farther in 1953 when, in that year, one of the most crackpot ideas of all time was foisted upon a submissive majority in this house by the government. The proposal then was that instead of setting aside a fixed sum of money for the use of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or, better still, an annual grant, there should be placed rather at the disposal of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the proceeds, whatever they might be, of the revenues derived under the provisions of the Excise Tax Act from the tax on radio and television receiving sets and tubes. It was a harebrained idea from the beginning. It was the kind of idea that defeats all attempts at parliamentary control and is bound to limit all
lMr. Fleming.]

sense of responsibility to parliament on the part of a government agency.
The first proposal was that the estimated $6 million revenue available from the tax on radio receiving sets would be placed at the disposal of the corporation for development of sound broadcasting. It was estimated that there would be $6 million a year available from the tax on television receiving sets and tubes and it was proposed that that revenue would go to the corporation for the development of television. That estimate looked to be too exact or too precise and so, although that was the first proposal made by the then minister of finance in the session of 1953, before we reached the details of it the government decided that they did not want that line of division drawn; they wanted the fund mingled. So what we have is simply an omnibus provision that total revenue derived under the Excise Tax Act from the tax on radio receiving sets and television receiving sets and tubes of both kinds should be placed at the disposal of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation indiscriminately.
At the time we said that was no way in which to estimate needs and that it would be no time at all before those revenues would bear little or no relation to the actual needs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. In that respect our predictions have been justified 100 per cent. Unlike the provision made in 1951 for the five-year grant, this time these provisions were placed at the disposal of the corporation in perpetuity, and, until the government introduces a specific bill in this house for that purpose, the house is powerless to interfere with the allocation of these revenues to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, regardless of whether the amount be small or whether it be, as it is today, very much larger than was originally estimated.
As compared with the estimate given to us in 1953, the revenue yielded in the fiscal year 1953-54 to the broadcasting corporation by the tax on television receiving sets and tubes was $11,703,000, practically double what was estimated in 1953. On the other hand, the revenue derived from the tax on radio receiving sets and tubes was $5 million. They were out by 16 per cent in that calculation. Now T.V. sets are being purchased at a rate where this tax is yielding the corporation currently at the rate of approximately $23 million a year. It is a mistake to follow the figures given in the book of estimates on page 10, where the estimate of revenue from this tax for the year 1955-56 is given as $18 million. It is obvious that last year's estimate of $15 million was much below the actual revenue. This estimate of $18 million for the new fiscal

year will be too low as well. As I indicated, while the sale of television sets in 1954 was 70 per cent greater than in 1953, the figures we have available for 1955 already show an increase in January of 60 per cent in the sales of television sets this year over those in January, 1954. It is therefore obvious that the C.B.C., under this omnibus provision of revenue, is going to derive a much larger figure than that given in the estimates, a larger figure even than the swollen figure of last year.
Hence we see a situation where the C.B.C. is in receipt of lush revenues beyond the control of parliament. In this respect I ask specifically that the estimates on page 10 of the book of estimates under the heading "Canadian Broadcasting Corporation" all be referred to this proposed select committee for review.
I now come to the subject of surplus. In its annual report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954-which is the last date for which we have any report from the corporation-we find the corporation reporting that it has shown for the fiscal year 1953-54 what it calls an operating surplus of $6,500,000. An operating surplus! What a misnomer! What a fiction, Mr. Speaker! An operating surplus suggests good management, thrift and care. But what do we find here? The revenues of the corporation were $27,431,000, of which 84 per cent was derived from taxation. They spent $19.9 million. They charged up also $1 million depreciation and arrived at this so-called operating surplus of $6,500,000. What that ought to be called is the extent to which, under misleading government policies, there has been placed at the disposal of the corporation far too much money beyond parliamentary control, thereby constituting, as it inevitably does, an invitation to spend.
I hope that hon. members of this house read the press report issued by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in December at the time it made public its annual report, this annual report that shows that the corporation last year had placed at its disposal $6,500,000 more than it could possibly find ways of spending. I would ask them to note, if they will, what the corporation had to say in trying to sound blue and pessimistic in the face of that statement. Here is what they said:
"Revenues based on sales of sets, however, cannot be expected to rise much further, and will probably drop in the future," the report said. "At the same time, however, operating costs will inevitably rise steeply as the system spreads across the country and as program production develops". (Revenues for the current year are expected to just about cover expenditures.)
Special Committee on Broadcasting
Sir, that was put out at a time when the revenues were going up by leaps and bounds as sales of television sets were outrunning those of 1953 by 70 per cent, and now in 1955 are outrunning even 1954 figures by 60 per cent. It is evident that this system of putting unfixed revenues at the disposal of the corporation has just run wild.
Is it any wonder then that all through the years we are seeing a continued rise in expenditure by the corporation now outrunning anything that anybody could have foreseen a few years ago? Back in 1937 the corporation was spending less than $1 million a year. In the years through the war its expenditures rose first to $3 million and then at the close of the war to about $51 million expenditure each year. By 1949 they had reached $71 million, 1950 $8 million, 1951 $91 million, 1952 $111 million, and fop the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953, $15 million, and last year ended March 31, 1954, if you include depreciation, nearly $21 million. Yes, we are in big figures now, big money. For that reason, sir, there is more need than ever before for strict parliamentary control of these expenditures and of the funds placed at the disposal of the corporation.
At the same time the corporation has gone on in these recent years borrowing money from the government. It is the government's fault. Borrowing has been made too easy for the corporation. Over the whole period of time total loans made by the government to the corporation have aggregated $20,900,000. Repayments, and none of them are in recent years, aggregated $1,900,000. There are today outstanding indebtednesses of the corporation to the government aggregating $19 million. Of that total the amount made available by parliament by loans for television development is $15,750,000, and for sound broadcasting $3,250,000.
Even while parliament was increasing by these huge amounts the revenues placed at the disposal of the corporation the government was fostering loans to the corporation. In 1953 there was a loan of $4,750,000, in 1954 another loan of $3 million, at the very time that in that fiscal year the corporation was showing $6| million that had not been spent, over and above its actual outlays. If you take off the $1 million charged for depreciation, the corporation in the fiscal year 1953-54 had enough money available to do everything that it required to do without one cent of these two loans aggregating $7| million.
The government would not listen to us. They chose to encourage this borrowing at the very time when the corporation had all the liquid assets it needed to meet all its

Special Committee on Broadcasting outlays. At the same time there has been no encouragement given to repaying any of these loans when these so-called operating surpluses have existed. Rather, the corporation has gone on paying interest to the government actually in excess of the amount earned on the government bonds that the corporation holds and in which it has invested its surpluses of money. Apparently the policy is to get hold of all the money you can, get hold of it now, get it as far away from parliamentary control as possible and then apply the good old rule-what we have we hold.
Sir, the Auditor General had something to say also about this statement of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to which I have referred. Mr. Watson Sellar, in his report to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) dated August 5, 1954, had this to say:
Having completed the audit of the accounts of the above-noted corporation for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954, I now report to you, in compliance with the requirements of section 87 of the Financial Administration Act the results of the examination both of the accounts, and of the financial statement forwarded herewith.
Allowance for depreciation and obsolescence.
May I remind the house here that $1 million was charged up for that purpose in the statement to which he is referring, and but for that charge this so-called operating surplus would have been $74 million instead of $6J million. I continue:
Still applicable is the comment in previous reports to the effect that the appropriateness of the accumulated allowance for depreciation and obsolescence is open to question for the reason that the rates used through the years have never been scientifically established or consistently applied.
Weaknesses having been noted in the accounts, this office wrote to the chairman of the board of governors on October 23, 1952 with supporting details and concluding with the words:	. . it is
suggested that the system be carefully reviewed, and appropriately revised and co-ordinated so that there may be no need to aualify the audit certificate in this regard". Subsequent action by the corporation not having been of a nature to remedy the situation, the manner in which the accounts were kept during the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954 was not found to be conducive to satisfactory audit.
Subject to the foregoing. I certify that, in my opinion-
Then he goes on with his certificate. The corporation in its press statement has made a comment on the report of the Auditor General, and in fairness I wish to read it. It is short. It reads:
The letter from the Auditor General on page 51 of the report mentions the "manner in which the accounts were kept". This is understood to refer to the technical system on which the accounts have been based. Since its foundation, the corporation has used a "modified cash basis" for its accounts, as do most government bodies. The


Auditor General is of the opinion that the corporation's cash system of accounting should be changed to an accrual system, as used by most companies at the present time. The C.B.C. is at present studying this suggestion. It has asked a firm of chartered accountants to advise on the practicality of carrying out a change to an accrual basis and the extra costs that would be involved.
Sir, the only comment I have to make on that is to ask this question. Why did the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation wait until the fall of 1954 to undertake a study of something that had been drawn to their attention and condemned by the Auditor General away back in 1952? If this matter warranted its reference to an independent firm of auditors for their advice in 1954, why was it not so referred by the corporation when they received the Auditor General's letter back in October, 1952? This is the sort of looseness and carelessness that will inevitably arise, that is inevitably encouraged as long as huge sums of money are irresponsibly placed by the government at the disposal of the corporation.
I have this comment to make with respect to the financing policies that are being followed today by the government, and here I am speaking strictly within the realm of government policy. Last night the minister quite properly drew attention to the realm of responsibility of the government as opposed to that field within which the corporation operates. But here we are speaking about something that is strictly within the realm of government policy. That policy is dangerous and unsound. What we say is that the proper course, the only course that any parliament ought to take that is mindful of its responsibilities to the public and to the public funds, is to meet the needs of the broadcasting corporation annually by an annual grant based upon proven annual needs.
Parliament should never make grants in advance available, as in the case of the five-year program, without further reference to parliament. Parliament should not make available to the corporation or to any other government agency the proceeds of any particular tax which may fluctuate from year to year and which, as is already seen in the case of the tax on television receiving sets, has run now to figures far greater than were foreseen by anyone in the house when that legislation was passed in 1953.
The policy of the Conservative party is to retain and assert strict parliamentary control over these large public expenditures. We believe in the policy of making an annual grant after an annual review. We hold the government responsible for the sad results, the costly results, of putting lavish sums of

money at the disposal of the corporation in a manner designed to further the monopolistic policies of the government and to escape parliamentary control.

I rise, Mr. Speaker, to support the motion to set up a committee to study the operations of the C.B.C., and to look into the new problems which are posed by television, as well as to examine, as we have in other years, the details in connection with radio broadcasting. The committee will study the reports of the C.B.C. itself, and I have no doubt will study also such briefs as are presented by the private broadcasting association. I may say I do not take as black a view of C.B.C. television and radio broadcasting as does my hon. friend who has just spoken. I would, at the outset, say that we of the C.C.F. generally-and the emphasis is on that word -support the policy of the C.B.C. and support the policy of the government in its operation of the C.B.C.
I may turn my attention for a moment to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. I always envy the hon. member for Eglinton because of his facility with words. If my hon. friend had been a Greek runner and had been running a marathon race, he would have kept on going even if someone had pushed the finish line back five miles. He would never even notice it. I might go so far as to say that if the track were circular he might even run over the same ground without noticing it. However, that is merely by way of jest, and we must discuss this subject sensibly.
I should like to examine one or two of the arguments put forward by the hon. member before proceeding to say what I had intended to say myself. The hon. member for Eglinton made a point of the fact that the private stations are in competition with the C.B.C., or perhaps I should put it the other way about, that the C.B.C. is in competition with the private stations. I shall say a word or two about that later. He asserted also that there is too much power in the hands of this one government agency. Before going farther, I would say, too, that my friend asserted the Conservative party has been consistent in the policy which he enunciated today. I do not believe he would object if I reminded him that in Hansard for May 11, 1932, page 2826, we find this:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the constitution of a commission to be known as the Canadian radio broadcasting commission, for the purpose of acquiring, operating, regulating and controlling radio broadcasting in Canada.
1823
Special Committee on Broadcasting
My hon. friend, of course, has heard that quotation before, because it is a resolution that was introduced by his own party's government.
The hon. member has suggested that we should have another regulatory body, a body which would have control not only over the operations of the private stations but over the C.B.C. itself. My friend did not say who was likely to be appointed to that body, by whom the body should be appointed, nor did he say, as I had hoped he would because I would have been interested, why he thought such a controlling body would be better or more efficient than the body we now have. I feel the hon. member is wrong in assuming a basis of equality when he asserts the C.B.C. is simply a competitor of the private stations. I deny that. So far as I can see, the only justifiable reason one could advance for the appointment of such board as he suggests would be that the C.B.C. now is being unjust to these private stations which my hon. friend asserts are its competitors. I do not believe that the C.B.C. is, as my hon. friend has said, une menace a la liberte. I do not believe the freedom of the individual is interfered with very much because of the fact we have a publicly-controlled corporation in charge of radio and television. On the other hand, I think such an organization protects the liberty of the individual, particularly in regard to freedom of speech, as I shall attempt to show later in these remarks.
I sometimes wonder if my hon. friend-* I have no means of knowing-is perhaps not more interested in the private enterprise interests in radio and television than he is concerned with the freedom of the individual, or indeed with the public good. I make no such charge. I merely put forward the query. My friend then proceeded to find some objection to a particular program. I shall not discuss that because I feel that is precisely the reason this committee is being established, so we may look into these individual grievances and complaints. May I say that I have some of them to offer myself. I suppose most of us will be asking critical questions, and all of us I am sure are anxious that the C.B.C. should be efficient and should be performing those functions for which it was created.
My hon. friend made a good deal of the point that too small a percentage of our television programs are of Canadian content. At this particular stage, with a young organization or at least an organization which is now involved in something new, I doubt if that is a fair criticism. It is hardly fair to expect that overnight, or in the course of a year or

Special Committee on Broadcasting two, the C.B.C. should have developed a series of Canadian programs with which it could fill its whole time upon the air. Such is the demand for television today, one would naturally expect that the C.B.C. would he forced to use, in addition to its own programs, such good programs as it could obtain elsewhere. May I say that I, personally, have a good deal of confidence in the judgment of the board of governors of the C.B.C. and of the president of that board, perhaps a good deal more confidence than I would have in certain other people who would like to foe directing the television and radio stations in this country.
I, of course, am completely in agreement with my hon. friend when he states he would like to see more programs of Canadian origin. I do not believe anyone will disagree with that. My hon. friend makes a great point of certain quotations that he gave us, and I suppose many which he did not give us, from the Massey commission report. If one examines the recommendations of the Massey commission as a whole, I believe he will find they are fairly consistently in favour of control of radio and television by the corporation.
There is one point on which I must violently disagree with my hon. friend, and that is when he criticizes the selection of certain talks or programs by the C.B.C. as being too much to the left, or too much in some other direction. I am in favour of freedom of speech; I am in favour of freedom of the intellect; I am in favour of intellectual integrity; I am in favour of hearing all sides of any question. And it is precisely because I am in favour of such things that I favour the existence of a regulatory body such as the C.B.C., responsible to parliament, responsible to the representatives of the people of Canada, who are in a position to insist and to see to it that all sides of any question are placed upon the air.
I hesitate to refer to my hon friend's assertion about the communist party. I have as little use for the communist party as he has; but I am suggesting that when any political party is not given the opportunity to make its beliefs known, then by that very method we are adopting the procedure they would follow if they were in power.
I do not believe, as some of my hon. friends in other parts of, the house believe, that there is at this moment in Canada any considerable communist menace. But I am going to suggest that if hon. members want to create one, or to drive the one we now have underground, this is precisely the very best way to do it.


Those are some of the arguments advanced by the hon. member, and on the spur of the moment I have answered them as best I can. I should like for a moment now to deal with the fact that undoubtedly we will be receiving again a brief from private broadcasters in Canada, in which they will advance their usual assertion that they are cramped, cabined, cribbed and confined by the actions of the regulatory body, the C.B.C.
I think it is perfectly proper that the private broadcasters should be heard, and if they have a case it should be considered carefully. But I do suggest that in my opinion their grievance in the past has always been based upon a wrong assumption, the assumption that, under the law, broadcasting is an industry. So far as I am concerned, broadcasting is not an industry. It is a public service which should be directed and controlled in the public interest by a public body responsible to the people. And the best body I know to do that is parliament.
Apparently that was the way Mr. Bennett wanted it, if the quotation to which I have referred means what it says. It was laid down in the act and, so far as I am concerned, that is the way it should be. I would say that the C.B.C. is not merely a competitor of the private broadcasting stations. It is not merely a commercial rival, as they would like to have people believe. And the C.B.C. must not be reduced to that level in public opinion.
I suggest that my hon. friend's demand for an independent regulatory authority is merely the thin edge of the wedge which would have the effect of prying the C.B.C. loose from the control it now exercises, thus reducing it to the status of a mere competitor; and indeed it might destroy it.
I am not suggesting to the hon. member for Eglinton that the purpose of the Conservative party is to destroy the C.B.C.; but I am suggesting that, if put into effect, the policy he proposes might in fact have that result. I have seen television in several parts of the world; I have seen it in Great Britain, and I like the British system. Of course the system in Great Britain has been established for a long time, and they have had the time to develop those things which we in Canada are only beginning to create. I do believe however that their programming, speaking generally, is superior to ours; and it is manifestly and tremendously superior to that of the United States. When I say that I am speaking in general terms because, of course, some of the finest programs I have ever seen have been put on by American stations.

Special Committee on Broadcasting
In Great Britain they started out with a public system such as we have here. I know my friends to my right will be quick to tell me that there has been some change in that regard, and that private stations are going to take over to some extent. Well, one might expect that with a Conservative government in power.
I see, however, that already the government in the United Kingdom is worried about the regulations which they feel will have to be placed upon the private stations. Only the other day I read a dispatch that said Mr. Churchill was worried about the fact that stations might use their new-found freedom to discuss, for instance, matters about to come up in the House of Commons, or perhaps even matters that had reached the order paper at Westminster. So it would seem that even Mr. Churchill thinks there is need for some regulation, in the public interest.
I do not want anyone to think, sir, that because I say these things I do not believe that private stations have a function to perform. On the contrary, I think they have a very useful function to perform, and that some of them are performing that function very well indeed. It is clear however that some are doing it much better than others.
One of my chief interests in radio and television is their cultural and educational influence. I was glad the minister said last night in his speech that we have the responsibility for what television does to our Canadian homes. I would translate that statement, in terms of education, and say that the cultural and educational influence the radio has upon the minds of our people is our business. And of course television has a much greater influence, I should imagine, than has radio broadcasting, because people spend more time looking at television than listening to the radio.
I believe that having a broadcasting corporation in control of radio broadcasting from coast to coast promotes national unity. I believe it is a good thing for the country to have a corporation of that kind. Perhaps the minister had that in mind when he said in his opening speech that television should join Canadians together in better understanding.
It will be our business in the committee to see that these fine aspirations as expressed by the minister are carried out. I believe the fact that we have an institution like the C.B.C. helps to keep us distinctly Canadian-and that is one of the great arguments that can be used.
I have had some experience in the field of education, and I am well aware of the flood
of foreign-American, if you like-literature, motion pictures, comic strips, radio and television broadcasts that are bombarding us continually from the south side of the international boundary. I have nothing against our fine American neighbours, but we do not need to imitate them in every way in order to respect them. Surely it should be our objective to retain some of our own individuality, something of distinctiveness in our Canadian culture, whether it arises from our English-speaking or our French-speaking background.
I suggest that simply to throw our broadcasting into the hands of commercial interests -because that is what we would be doing if we abandoned the whole philosophy of the C.B.C. idea-would leave no doubt as to where our programs would be coming from. They are all ready for us there, packed up in a box as it were, with soapsuds at one end and culture at the other. We would simply import them here; and because no private interest could afford to create Canadian programs for the sake of creating Canadian programs we would be bound by necessity to commercialism and vulgar commercialism in most cases.
It has been difficult to keep out these United States influences which I assert are harmful in some respects, this because of the greater wealth and influence of our neighbours to the south. As I say, this influence is exerted by newspapers and magazines, but if we could counteract it somehow by the use of Canadian programs then I think we would be doing a good piece of work. We need programs which are inspired not by money or commercial interests but simply by the desire to promote the education and culture of our own country.
There is another thing I want to mention, something about which I have spoken before, and that is freedom of speech. Considering the time I have available I shall not repeat the things I have said before. I am sure my hon. friends to my right are quite sincere, but on other occasions in the radio committee they have objected to certain programs. I am thinking of one scientific program to which they objected. I look upon that as being the same as a program by any political party or any minority group. I believe in hearing all sides of a question. We want to hear every side and have the freedom to form our own opinions. It is a poor cause that cannot stand on its own feet. It is a poor cause which has to be kept in the dark for fear somebody might examine it. Let us bring the thing out in the open.
