If there is anything good in it, let us have it; if it is bad in our opinion, let us reject it. But let us hear it. I do not care
1826	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Broadcasting whether it is a certain scientific program or whether it is the opinions of some crazy political party, let us hear them all.
My hon. friend said we should suppress the opinions of a certain political party and not permit them to speak over the radio. I am going to ask him to consider this. If, and God forbid, the communist party ever gained power by the ballot, what chance does he think the Conservative party would have of getting free time on the air over the C.B.C.? I am afraid my hon. friend is following the exact line which he deplores in others. If he will think the matter through I believe he will realize that I am right.
Does my hon. friend suggest that the communists in this country, the labour progressive party so-called, should have free time on a national network?

As long as any political party comes within the regulations as set down by law, then I say that party has a right to be heard. If we change the law-and it will be over my dead body that we abandon the principle of free speech-that is another matter. But I am submitting that as the matter now stands and as, thank God, we have freedom in this country, we should try to keep it. That is the best answer I can make at the moment.
I think even those radio programs that we get now have too much commercialism in them. In other words, these corporations or these people who want to sell soap-they first sell us the filth and then they sell us the soap-should not be dictating to us what type of program we are going to listen to. That is why I am glad there is still in this country a body which is to a degree independent of soap, such as the C.B.C.
May I ask my hon. friend which body in this country is independent of soap?

My hon. friend reminds me of an advertisement which appeared in Punch. I recommend this to the Minister of National Health and Welfare for use in his clean-up campaign. This showed an old whiskered tramp who was saying, "Last year I used Pears' soap and since then I have used no other". I do not know whether my hon. friend would put me in that category.
Who airs the soap operas in Canada?

Am I also not allowed to criticize the C.B.C.? I am ready to criticize any program which contains too much commercialism. Of course the C.B.C. will say they have to get the financial wherewithal.
IMr. Knight.]

I am hoping that under the new set-up-I am appealing to the C.B.C. on that basis-we will not be victimized so much by having these commercial programs, that we will have more of these sustaining programs, if that is the right term.
I prefer to have the choice of programs in the hands of a body such as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is under the control of this parliament, rather than in the hands of commercial interests whose sole motive, or at least whose main motive, is that of profit.
These are some of the reasons I support C.B.C. policy, and why I support this government in this particular operation. I cannot be accused of doing this too often, and it is perhaps a refreshing change for me to be able to rise and not be opposing the government. May I say that I get much more satisfaction from being a member of the opposition. My hon. friend opposite who is sitting waiting to make a smart remark will probably tell me that I shall have that experience for some time. However, I have anticipated him.
I emphasize again that whoever is to control television in this country must be responsible to this House of Commons, as far as I am concerned. We now have a system of public control with the regulation of private stations. We do not want to have a repetition of what has happened in radio and television in the United States, where the programming is largely in the hands of the advertisers and is controlled by them.
I could take time to speak about the development of Canadian talent. I feel certain that under the present arrangement a good many more people will be trained to sing, act and perform in other ways. These are the kind of things people like to hear on the air and see on the screen. More people would be trained in this way than under another system.
The private stations, of course, have been increasing their power. I think possibly there should be some criticism of the C.B.C. in the committee due to the fact that the private stations have perhaps been allowed to increase their power too much. I would remind you, sir, that the increased power and wealth and the increased operation which they are enjoying have come about by an act of grace and not by any right. One only has to study the Radio Act to discover that this is true. I do not propose to argue the point because I do not know enough about the technical aspects of it, but they have been allowed to increase their wave lengths and have been given more power than they had before. I would repeat that

they "have these privileges by an act of grace and not by any right given to them under the Radio Act.
I believe my opening words were to the effect that I have lent general support to the C.B.C. and to the government in respect of its operations. But I suggest there should be no smugness on the part of the minister, the government or the C.B.C. itself. We shall be watching in that committee for any tendencies, as I suggested, to deviate from the path of public control. We shall ask, I hope, critical questions. We shall endeavour to insist upon efficiency in operation in return for support from public funds. We shall hope the operations will be carried out in accordance with the policies laid down by the minister in his speech, parts of which I have already quoted.

I was rather hoping that the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) would continue to speak and consume a little more of the time left before adjournment so I would not have to start on the quarter hour.
Generosity.
I would like to be able to finish my speech by five o'clock, and I do not like to ask permission to adjourn the debate. Would you care to call it five o'clock, or shall I proceed?
Proceed.

I am glad that once again we have an opportunity of carrying on this debate concerning Canada's radio policy. We are happy that a special committee on radio broadcasting is to be set up at this session.
I have listened to the previous speakers with great interest. I listened to the Minister of National Revenue who is sort of a liaison officer between the crown corporation, the C.B.C., and the government, but I do not think I gained anything that was particularly new from his remarks except' that he did bring us up to date on the achievements of the C.B.C. in respect to television.
I listened to the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) who made, I think, a critical but good analysis of the present radio situation in Canada with respect to the C.B.C. I also listened with interest to the hon. member who preceded me, the hon. member for Saskatoon. I always enjoy his speeches, but I must say that he has followed the same line the socialist party of Canada has followed for a good many years in respect to radio policies. It is quite obvious that he is a great supporter of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the policy it follows today. He follows in the footsteps of his leader and of
8,	1955
Special Committee on Broadcasting those in the C.C.F. party who have spoken at any time concerning this matter. They all follow the same line.
I have criticized the C.B.C. in the past and have felt that it has had socialist leanings in regard to its policies generally. I have said that before and I say it again. The fact that our C.C.F. friends to a man lean over backward in supporting the C.B.C. is a dead giveaway. As a matter of fact, the minister listens and appears to me to sit back with a good deal of satisfaction as the C.C.F. appear to be throwing the Liberal spitballs. When asked a question, my hon. friend from Saskatoon rose and with great gusto asked if he did not have the right to criticize the C.B.C. Of course he had that right, but what was his criticism? The only thing he criticized were the soap operas. Well, I do not think the soap operas are as bad as all that. I do not listen to them very often, I must confess, but my wife does and I believe a lot of old women do, but even if they do-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You had better straighten that out in a hurry.
What a brave man you are.
I was not referring to my wife.
Now you are trying to hedge.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Whose wife were you referring to?	[DOT]
I am very proud of my wife. She is a very charming lady.
Hear, hear.
So are we.

I like to see her sit back with a good deal of satisfaction and listen to the soap operas. What is wrong with the soap operas? Is there anything particularly wrong with them? I do not listen to them. I think they are a lot of nonsense. They play on the heartstrings and contain a lot of sob stuff and revolve around the eternal triangle and that sort of thing. Seldom, however, do you find excessive drinking scenes in the soap operas. Seldom do you find bloodthirsty murders taking place in the soap operas. I do not think they are such terrible things after all. If that is all hon. members find to criticize I do not think the criticism is particularly well founded. I suggest that if the soap operas carried the same commercials but consisted of cleverly designed plays slanted toward the left, the hon. members would be praising them as among the greatest programs on the radio; yes, sir.
I should like to speak along a slightly different line this time. I shall perhaps be a bit philosophical in my speech this afternoon and this evening. As a basic question I

Special Committee on Broadcasting should like to ask what is the purpose of radio and television? I wonder whether we have ever faced up to that question and answered it. I think the purpose could be broken down into three divisions. I am going to mention three anyway, for the purpose of analysis. I am not mentioning them necessarily in the order of their importance. One of the purposes of radio and television is to entertain. Another purpose is to impart information and factual knowledge. If you like you can turn that phraseology around and say "factual information and knowledge". Another purpose is to guide and to encourage cultural activities. When you have said that I think you have just about answered the question as to the purpose of broadcasting.
Of course it costs money to broadcast, and naturally it may be a lucrative field. That depends on where the station may be located, the scope of the radio advertising that can be handled and all that sort of thing; but it cannot be done for nothing. I suppose it might be said that some people are in the business of broadcasting because it is a profitable business. But the actual answer to the real purpose of broadcasting-and I think this should be the policy of the C.B.C.-is to entertain, to impart factual information, understanding and knowledge and to guide and encourage cultural activities.
Let me analyse those three purposes for a moment, Mr. Speaker; and may I say that I am only giving you my own philosophical reasoning on the matter. First of all, suppose the purpose is to entertain. In that respect might I say that I believe television is gradually superseding radio broadcasting. That fact may not be too obvious at the present time but I believe that, apart from music that is tuned to the ear, there is perhaps no greater medium of entertainment than either live stage entertainment or that which may be observed over television. Television is a powerful medium. It is perhaps the most powerful medium devised by man for advertising and entertaining.
Right here might I say that this is where the local stations are so important. They are important because all people do not necessarily enjoy the same type of entertainment. I think we should do our best to localize entertainment, and to give the people the type of entertainment they want in their various localities. That does not, of course, do away with network radio broadcasting and television, because there are some types of programs that are enjoyed by everyone. But I believe we do a great service to this country if we pay special attention to broadcasting and television over local stations for the particular enjoyment and entertainment


of local audiences. There are differences in communities. Some communities are perhaps composed predominantly of certain ethnic groups. We do not all enjoy the same thing. We do not all look upon entertainment in the same light or give equal value to all types of entertainment. I therefore say we must pay special attention to the value of the entertainment angle of broadcasting and television on the local level.
In the second place, I stated that I thought one of the purposes of broadcasting was to impart factual information and knowledge. This is a subject upon which I have very definite convictions. Of course nobody knows everything and nobody has all the information. That is why we must analyse as accurately as possible just what we might mean by freedom of expression. I have listened to a good many talks that have been given on the networks of the C.B.C. over the years. I think we can conclude without any argument that opinions are not necessarily facts, but very often opinions can be so stated that they appear to be facts.
I note that Mr. Speaker is looking at the clock, and I might as well break off here as anywhere. I would therefore ask you, Mr. Speaker, to call it five o'clock.
On motion of Mr. Hansell the debate was adjourned.

Mr. Speaker, do I understand
that we are to convene here at 5.30?

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. McCann:
That a select committee be appointed on broadcasting to consider the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and to review the policies and aims of the corporation and its regulations, revenues, expenditures and development, with power to examine and inquire into the matters and things herein referred to and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and to send for persons, papers and records; that the committee have power to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be deemed advisable or necessary; that the committee have power to meet while the house is sitting; that the committee shall consist of the following members; Messrs. Balcer, Beaudry, Boisvert, Bryson, Carter, Cauchon, Decore, Diefenbaker, Dinsdale, Fleming, Gauthier (Portneuf), Gauthier (Nickel Belt), Goode, Hansell, Henry, Holowach, Kirk (Shelburne-Yarmouth - Clare), Knight, McCann, Monteith, Reinke, Richard (Ottawa East), Richardson, Robichaud, Studer, Weaver; that standing orders 64 and 65 be suspended in relation thereto.

Mr. Speaker, before the dinner adjournment I was dealing with a question which I asked at the very commencement of my remarks and then attempted to answer in a somewhat philosophical fashion. The question I asked was, what is the purpose of broadcasting? I stated that I thought the
question could be answered in three ways. The first purpose of broadcasting is to entertain, the second purpose is to impart factual information and knowledge, and the third purpose is the encouragement of cultural activity.
At the moment of adjournment I was dealing with the second purpose, the imparting of factual information and knowledge.
I stated that this is a subject upon which I have very definite convictions. I followed that by stating that usually the commentaries and talks that come over the radio-and I must say it appears to me that most of them come over the networks in Canada under the supervision of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-are, after all, opinions, and that opinions are not necessarily facts. I want to make that clear. But when these opinions are expressed over the air they do have all the colour of facts, and as people listen they absorb them and take them to be facts.
I should like to call attention to three examples. I have no particular speaker or speech in mind. Suppose, for instance, the C.B.C. should ask someone to speak on the root cause of unemployment. We may listen to this gentleman. He may be a scholar, he may be from a university, he may be a man holding some high executive post or he may be a big labour man, but when he speaks on the root cause of unemployment he is only expressing his opinion. Who is to say whether or not he is right? Who is to say whether or not it is factual? Yet the listening audience accepts what he says as factual.
Take the matter of international affairs. Commentators and speakers have spoken on the Far Eastern situation. Suppose a speaker should attempt to analyse the Formosan situation. Suppose he should go back into history and try to analyse the reasons for the communist revolution in China, trace the history of Chiang Kai-shek and so forth. That is opinion. It does not follow necessarily that it is factual. Yet those who are listening may easily absorb these opinions as though they were facts.
I have a pretty good illustration of that right here. The other day most of us received a letter from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) who was very greatly put out because something from Dr. James G. Endicott had been circularized to members of parliament, the title being
1830	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Broadcasting "Canadian Far Eastern News Letter". The Secretary of State for External Affairs was put out, and rightly so, and I want to thank him for the letter. But what did he say? He said that it was a vicious and grotesque misrepresentation of the true situation in Indo-China and simply unadulterated communist propaganda.
I use that as an illustration. As I say, I thank the minister for it. I was glad to get the letter, but I wonder what prompted the minister to send it. Does the minister think for one moment that members of parliament are so gullible as to swallow anything published by Dr. Endicott? Maybe some are. Personally I am not, because I know the source from which it comes. But I am not going to accuse Dr. Endicott of being dishonest. I am not going to accuse him of writing something he did not believe.
That is just an illustration. It did not come over the air, but it greatly agitated the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It could have come over the air. If it had come over the air I am quite certain that the minister or one of his colleagues would have begged for time on the C.B.C. to correct what had been said. However, if Dr. Endicott had spoken in that fashion over the air we could take it for what it was worth and most people would say, "Oh, well, he is a communist; he follows the communist line". But there is a bigger danger than Dr. Endicott on the air. The bigger danger arises because men take to the air whose opinions are half truths, and half truths are worse than lies. Men who are lauded to the skies as great commentators, as great authorities give talks to which no answer is given. If an answer is given it is in a very modified fashion.
So far as I am concerned personally-I cannot talk for my group on this matter-I believe this country would be better off if there were no talks department in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Any talks that come over the air are propaganda talks. The very nature of talk makes that so. For what purpose does one talk over the air? It is to tell something to the people. For what purpose does one tell the people something? It is to inform them or persuade them. There is no other purpose. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is the danger I see.
I come now to this matter of factual information and knowledge. We believe in freedom of expression. I am saying to you that if all expression has to be channelled through half a dozen men in the talks department of the C.B.C., with a pint of brains each, before it can go on the air, that is not what I call freedom of expression. If our free way of life means anything it means only one
[Mr. Hansell.l

thing, and that is the freedom of the individual. I know quite well that 15 million Canadian people cannot talk over the air, but we accentuate the problem when there is only one channel of national broadcasting and people have to sit on the sidelines and wait upon the C.B.C.'s pleasure to call upon them to speak. You can count on your fingers and toes those upon whom they call to speak. I say, Mr. Speaker, that we have not reached what is known as individual freedom unless every individual in the country has the right to express himself if he wishes to do so.
Once again I come to the value of the local broadcasting station. We have got into the habit of thinking everything must be done in a sort of mass way. I have heard the phrase used, mass thinking. Now, Mr. Speaker, there is no such thing as mass thinking. You, Mr. Speaker, are thinking right now, but you are thinking with your own mind and not anyone else's. The minister who sponsors this resolution is thinking with his own mind. He is mighty glad he is not thinking with mine.
Hear, hear.
When I think with my own mind, I am not thinking with his, thank God.
Hear, hear.

There is no such thing as mass thinking. It is individual thinking. There is no such thing as mass freedom. It is individual freedom. In that way we exalt the dignity of the individual, for it is the individual who is man indeed. My friend of the C.C.F. who preceded me said they thought that both sides of every question should be discussed, and intimated that we did not believe that. Of course we believe it, but the trouble is only one side of the question is put forward and the other side is left unspoken.
I enjoy listening to some of these things. I enjoy listening to that program "Press Conference", especially when my leader is the one being questioned because he has the ability to handle himself and others. As I have heard this "Press Conference" I have often thought that if we wanted to hear both sides of the question we should reverse the order on every other broadcast, and instead of having half a dozen newspapermen question one leader we should have six members of parliament question one newspaperman to see what he knows about the problem. These men report the doings of this house-

factual. Why should they not be on the receiving end of the questions occasionally? I should like to see that happen. I do not know whether we would get any truth, but I tell you we would have a lot of fun.
It might be said there are some subjects that are unpopular. Perhaps when giving out information, putting on talks and so forth, it might be said that we should deal with those things that are popular. Well, that might sound nice, but let me say this. All through the ages that which was unpopular was never received. Truth is never popular. The new which is displacing the old is never popular. In this old world righteousness is never popular. Now, Mr. Speaker, I leave those observations with you, and I say I have convictions along those lines.
The third purpose for radio broadcasting and television is the encouragement of cultural activity. Let us not fall overboard, or lean backward on something until we fall over. According to my philosophical thinking culture cannot be produced by any broadcasting company or any broadcasting station. So far as culture is concerned, that is something which is developed over a long, long period of time. By its very nature it is a matter of breeding. There was a lot of culture before we ever had radio. Culture cannot be stereotyped. There are different peoples in this world, all having different types of culture. Culture can only live, thrive and grow in an atmosphere of perfect individual freedom, when the whole personality has an opportunity of expressing itself. It might be in literature; it might be in art; it might be in music, but it is only when the individual personality has an opportunity of expressing itself that we come anywhere near attaining culture.
The Russians attempt to stereotype culture. My hon. friend from Edmonton East (Mr. Holowach) and I were in Montreal the other day, and we went to an exhibition of the works of Matisse. I am somewhat interested in painting, having taken some courses in art in my time, and I must say I enjoyed the exhibition of the works of Matisse. However, we went into another room where there were works that had nothing to do with Matisse. This was a room filled with modern painting-painted by surrealists, I believe they are called. It was a lot of dab-dab stuff, where they put a few lines here and a lot of paint there, and if you look at it long enough you think you see a woman's hand up here, and her foot sticking out somewhere else. I can never see any sense in it.
Finally we came to a picture which was nothing but a lot of daubs of paint. My hon. friend from Edmonton East turned to a lady
Special Committee on Broadcasting standing beside him and, in a jocular fashion -probably she did not know he was joking- he said, "What is that picture?" The lady looked at him and said, "Search me; it looks like a patchwork quilt to me." Another lady said, "I think it is there to express colour." You know, they will not permit that in Russia; no, they will not permit it. And why? Because they say it is degenerate. I do not know why they think it is degenerate; to me it is humorous.
I would not say for one moment that we should cramp an individual's style. If any individual thinks he is an artist, gets a tube of paint and-squish-squirts it on a board,- blobs it all over and then says, "That's modern art"-well, in a free society he should have the right to do it. And if he can get enough people around him to enjoy that type of art, I wish him good luck. He should be able to do it in a free society, if that is the expression of his personality.
I see I have only about five minutes left, and I shall close in that time. Before taking my seat, however, I would reiterate once more what we have said many times in the house and in the radio committee, that the C.B.C. should be placed upon a completely competitive basis, a basis on which it would be competitive with private stations. Let it prove itself; let it administer its affairs just the same as any other radio company, in competition with its competitors. It does not do that today, because it has control of its competitors.
I believe a second network should be operated by independent stations, and that the C.B.C. should be subsidized only to the extent of its services in Canada at points where no other service is given, and where it can be shown that such service is given for the encouragement of the cultural arts. I believe, too, that all regulatory authority should be stripped from the C.B.C. and placed in the hands of a separate regulatory body, or else the regulations should be written into the law.

Mr. Speaker, there is fundamental disagreement between the views of the hon. member for Eglinton and those I hold on this question. Two points should be kept in mind when discussing Canadian radio and television. First there is the public interest, which transcends private rights and which means of necessity that broadcasting and television must primarily be run in the interests of the Canadian people, and not primarily by private interests for profit.
Second, the geographical make-up of Canada and the fact that this is a bilingual country, in fact a country of many languages, also dictates the set-up we have today. My hon. friend may protest that he is willing to recognize the primacy of public interest, but a careful listening to his speech this afternoon convinced me that he would like to scrap the present set-up and turn over Canadian radio to the soap operas and the advertising jingles of the commercial hucksters.
I should like to comment briefly upon the hon. member's views on C.B.C. talks. I was particularly interested in his reference to the fact that most speakers favoured the government or represented views left of centre. Personally I have found that talks over the C.B.C. on international affairs are of an extremely high calibre. Consider, for example, a program like "Capital Report" which we hear every Sunday afternoon. Let us consider for a minute some of the speakers such as James McConachie of Time magazine, who speaks from Washington. Anyone associated with Time magazine could not be accused of having views which are anything but centre or right of centre.
Then again when we come to Canada we hear commentators such as Anne Francis, an independent commentator, and Mr. Blakely of the Montreal Gazette, which generally does not favour the government. He is ready to defend any shibboleth, to extol the orthodox, but to be careful of free and intelligent discussion. I think the best example of this line of thinking can be found in "Call to Greatness" by Adlai E. Stevenson, and I commend this magnificent series of

lectures to the attention of hon. members. At page 100 Mr. Stevenson has this to say: Unreason and anti-intellectualism abominate thought. Mr. Speaker, all hon. members taking part in this discussion thus far have indicated their pleasure that once again members are going to have an opportunity of peering into this very important avenue of public service in Canada. Because the C.B.C. operates as one of the numerous crown corporations I feel it is essential that parliament should have every possible opportunity to make a thorough examination and analysis of what has been going on since the committee last met.
In all the crown corporations which have been developed in Canadian government circles in recent years we find that we are faced with a definite tendency toward increasing secrecy. From time to time in this house we hear complaints that it is becoming increasingly difficult for private members, particularly those outside the government group, to obtain complete information as to what is taking place in these corporations. This is especially dangerous in the field of communication.
It is a well known truism that whenever autocracy or authoritarianism raises its ugly head the first move made is to take over, with very rigid control, the various media of communication in the country. Because of this, Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity of once again seeing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's policies and activities brought under review by the parliamentary committee.

Special Committee on Broadcasting
Broadcasting in Canada as well as in other countries has developed quickly. The first broadcasting licence was granted to the Marconi corporation in the year 1919. Since that time there has been a tremendous and almost revolutionary development in this important media of communication. Unfortunately in Canada the pace of development has been so rapid that it has been hardly possible for parliamentary and governmental policy to keep abreast of the technological changes.
Several hon. members in this debate have referred to the fact that the pattern for broadcasting was laid down by the Aird commission in 1932. I believe it was the hon. member from Saskatoon who referred to the position taken by the leader of the Conservative party at that time. I would like to suggest that the policy which applied to broadcasting in the year 1932 does not necessarily fit the reality of the situation as we find it in Canada at the present time. Indeed, if we had continued along the lines of the policy established by the Aird commission we would have been very backward in the development of broadcasting in Canada.
The Aird commission visualized the complete domination of the broadcasting medium by the C.B.C. or the Canadian broadcasting commission, as it was called at that time. It also visualized the eventual withering away of private broadcasting, which had already appeared on the scene in Canada. Instead of that we have seen a rapid and remarkable growth in the activity, the influence and the contribution of the private broadcasters in Canada. The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) suggested that the very geographic circumstances in Canada necessitate a continuing governmental monopoly on broadcasting. Rather, I would suggest, those geographic factors have worked toward a gradual whittling down of the domination of broadcasting by state monopoly.
In the few remarks I wish to make in this discussion tonight I want to underline some of the extremely helpful contributions by the private broadcasters that have been made to the past two parliamentary committees on broadcasting in which I have been privileged to participate. I have listened to the presentations of the C.A.B. on these two occasions, and I am convinced that they bring sensible opinions and ideas before the parliamentary committee.
The hon. member for Saskatoon spoke very strongly this afternoon in favour of maintaining a complete state monopoly on broadcasting. That is to be expected from the group he supports, because state control is basic to socialism. The private broadcasters
[Mr. Dinsdale.l

are in the position of beggars in the area of Canadian broadcasting. I sometimes feel they lack the prestige and influence which their demonstrated contribution to Canadian broadcasting activity merits. For example, the criticism has often been made that private stations have not made a worth-while contribution to the development of Canadian talent in the technical field, the field of programming and in the artistic field of Canadian broadcasting.
I am certain that if we were to examine the personnel rosters of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation today, we would find that a great many of the top level personnel in broadcasting had their beginning as announcers and participants in programs in the private, local community stations. This, of course, is as it should be.
Actually the small community stations operated by private broadcasters have been the only source for the development of technical skill. This is mainly due to the fact that in Canada we lack facilities for formal technical training by which young Canadians can be prepared for service in this important medium.
If it had not been for private broadcasters we would have been deficient in radio service in the smaller local communities. Without exception the small communities are served by private broadcasting stations. Because they are restricted to the local community and surrounding area they tend to reflect real Canadian life more accurately. I feel that because the C.B.C. has restricted its operations to the larger centres and has established its stations in cities such as Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg and Vancouver, it has become farther removed from the actual, cultural reality of Canada, and that the private broadcasting stations are closer to this reality.
There have been changes during the past two decades since national broadcasting was established in Canada. It is fortunate that these changes have gradually been following the right direction. The rapid development of broadcasting has made this necessary. When I first became interested in this problem there was tremendous antipathy toward what we call crass commercialism in Canadian broadcasting. That subject has been discussed from time to time during the debate today. It seems that soap operas are the bete noire of modern broadcasting. The last speaker, the hon. member for York Centre, seemed to imply that the monopoly control of the C.B.C. has saved us from a deluge of the type of emotional bilge which comes over the air waves in these soap operas. No doubt he is aware, as was brought out in

the question I put to the hon. member for Saskatoon, that any soap operas aired over Canadian radio today are broadcast by the C.B.C., and therefore any argument in that regard is without effect.
Actually we are not so much afraid of crass commercialism now as we were in the days of the infancy of broadcasting. Radio commercials are considerably removed from the earlier primitive forms. In some instances radio commercials have been elevated to somewhat of an art. I suppose the only real survivor of the early primitive form is the soap opera type of commercial which is aired regularly and daily by the C.B.C. stations.
A second interesting development has taken place in Canadian broadcasting. It would appear that the resistance to programs of United States origin has diminished to a certain extent. This is something that has happened particularly since the advent of television, I suppose mainly because C.B.C. television has been obliged to depend rather heavily upon United States sources for its program material. I also like to feel this is an indication that Canada has become more secure in its nationhood.
From the very beginning of broadcasting development in Canada the danger of saturation from United States sources has been raised as a bogey. It was felt that the United States, with its early start in broadcasting and with its huge financial and population resources, would completely absorb any purely Canadian expression of broadcasting north of the 49th parallel. The complaint of cultural adulteration by United States materialism has often been raised and is still raised as a red herring technique to obscure the real state of affairs.
Actually those who have given serious study to the influence of broadcasting and telecasting on the national mind have come to the conclusion that its effect is relatively superficial, and that the basic social institutions are still the chief source of cultural development in Canada. In fact one of the great authorities-I have raised this point before-the late Harold Innis of the University of Toronto, came to the conclusion that radio and television were essentially mechanized means of communication, and as a result had little effect on the development of real culture in the nation so long, of course, as the basic social institutions were strong.	.
There has been another shift or gradual change in Canadian broadcasting policy. It is related to the one I have just mentioned. The chairman of the C.B.C. board in a press interview recently, I was interested to note,

Special Committee on Broadcasting subscribed to this same opinion. The C.B.C. seems to be abandoning its attempt to elevate and to dictate taste, a project which was one of the early rigid policies laid down. In fact, in this press interview the chairman of the board, Mr. Davidson Dunton, said something to the effect that he is not particularly interested in this matter of elevating and dictating taste; he maintained that the primary function of the C.B.C. in this regard is to present a balanced program.
I think that is coming to a more common-sense and reasonable approach. After all, how can any centralized medium of communication, particularly when it is concentrated in urban areas, satisfy the variety of cultural and entertainment tastes that exist in this tremendous geographic territory we call Canada? Certainly there must be a fundamental cleavage between the urban and the rural areas. There is also the regional problem. As I have already indicated, it is because the private broadcasters operate in the local communities that they have tended to meet the real needs of those communities more closely than have the C.B.C. studios which are concentrated in the huge industrial cities scattered across Canada.
Finally, as to the changes that have gradually, almost unconsciously, taken place, may I say that there has been a moving away from the viewpoint that broadcasting is a natural monopoly. This viewpoint was reiterated tonight by the hon. member for York Centre, but there are few specialists in the field today who will subscribe to the belief that there is a natural monopoly because of the limited facilities for broadcasting, particularly since the advent of frequency modulation. Actually in Canada today there are more radio outlets than newspaper outlets. I am sure that in the not too far distant future we shall see the proliferation of stations in the telecasting field. It must be conceded that the C.B.C. or the government have not yet admitted the invalidity of the argument supporting a complete monopoly in broadcasting by this natural monopoly theory, but the fact is that the circumstances of broadcasting are moving inevitably toward a breaking down of this continuing monopoly position. I believe the persistence of the private broadcasters, as they have appeared time and time -again before parliamentary committees, is in good part responsible for the gradual change in thinking on the part of the Canadian public as well as on the part of the government and parliament as a whole.
As we come to another parliamentary committee on broadcasting, there are two changes that I think might well be considered during its deliberations. These have already been mentioned by several hon. members who have

Special Committee on Broadcasting spoken. In fact they have been mentioned in debates in the house during past years. As I refer once again to this subject of an independent regulatory body I want to emphasize at the outset that because this group is advocating such a body, that does not imply that we are advocating the removal of all regulation. That was the inference drawn by the hon. member for Saskatoon this afternoon.
Of course that is far from the truth. Any modern state, whether it be the United Kingdom or the United States-and the United States has the maximum of freedom in broadcasting-has of necessity found it essential to set up a regulatory body. The point we are putting forward, that is being put forward by an increasingly large number of individual citizens as well as citizens organized in groups, is the appeal for an independent regulatory body.
The hon. member for Eglinton referred to the recent resolutions of young Liberal organizations across the country. I should like to suggest to the government that the younger wings of political parties in Canada today tend to be very much closer to public opinion than the senior officials of political organizations. That applies particularly to a party that has been in power over a long period of years. When the young Liberals begin putting forward the suggestion, quite vociferously and enthusiastically, that the time has come in the development of Canadian broadcasting to take another step away from state domination of broadcasting, I think it is time for the government to pay attention.
The hon. member for Eglinton referred to some of the myths that have been shattered by certain C.B.C. television programs. As he was speaking it occurred to me that one myth that has not been shattered by C.B.C. operations is the myth of the infallibility of the Liberal party. I am not going to say there is any direct control or influence over Canadian broadcasting by the party in power, but it seems logical to assume that state domination of any mass media of communication offers very dangerous temptations indeed. In fact the temptations and dangers should be obvious. Certainly none of the important mass media, press, radio or television, should come under the control of politicians. I believe that is why public opinion in Canada is gradually being aroused in favour of an independent regulatory body.
As to the dangers of state domination of mass media, I had occasion recently to have some visitors come to Ottawa, and of course they wanted to sit in the gallery and watch parliament in action. They were particularly interested in seeing the members of the


cabinet. I asked them why they wanted to see the members of the cabinet in action, and one of the ladies in the group said it was because she thought they must be such wonderful men; they were always in the newspapers and always on the radio. I took my visitors to the gallery and they began their observation with a good deal of enthusiasm. As the evening wore on they became increasingly bored, and when they retired from the gallery said sadly; "They are only human beings, after all".
One reason, of course, why any authoritarian state wants to control radio or mass media of any kind is that they can so work on the attitudes and the minds of the citizenry as to almost establish the superman idea in the thinking of the public. There is no room for supermen in a democracy. I am reminded of an old adage that has been changed somewhat; some are born great, some have greatness thrust upon them; some achieve greatness, and some hire a press agent. In our modern, complex society it is amazing what you can do with a good press agent. Day after day as the leaders of Canadian public life have their speeches quoted in the press and repeated over the air, as their statements appear in the newsreels and finally in the week-end analysis of the news, the stereotype becomes established in the minds of the public that indeed these people must be exceptional and wonderful men.
Reference has already been made in this debate to the famous speech of the chairman of the board at Saskatoon last year, and rightly so, because it dealt with a very important subject pertaining to broadcasting. It seems that the chairman of the board is very keenly aware of the dangers of too much monopoly, particularly state monopoly, in the realm of radio broadcasting and telecasting. But I do not follow his argument all the way, because he feels that we in Canada are completely protected from any such dangers owing to the nature of the relationship between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the cabinet. However, because the corporation is a creature of the government, and particularly because the personnel of the board enjoy their tenure of office at the pleasure of the governor in council, there is a subtle, and sometimes not so subtle, control.
For example, so far as information is concerned, the minister responsible to the house for C.B.C. operations obviously is dependent upon the personnel of the C.B.C. for such information, and no doubt his thinking is shaped by the recommendations and suggestions that are put forward. I obtained a copy of a speech by the chairman of the C.B.C.

made on December 24 last over the C.B.C. in the form of a year-end report to the public of Canada concerning the activities of the corporation. In reading the speech and comparing it with the statement by the minister last evening one sees that there is a great deal in common, which indicates that there must be a rather close connection between this public corporation and the cabinet minister to which it is responsible.
I think the time has come, as indicated by the rising protest of public opinion, for the establishment of an independent regulatory body to supervise and regulate the activities of both the C.B.C. and private broadcasters in Canada. Today we cannot deny the fact that, contrary to what was expected when the broadcasting policy was first laid down, the private broadcasters have survived and have made a contribution to broadcasting in Canada which is of increasing importance to the development of our Canadian nationhood. I am sure they would be in a much more comfortable and certainly a much more creative position if they could be allowed to operate free from the shadow of rather close coercion by the group with which they are competing, because of the fact that the C.B.C., in addition to being their competitor, is also their adjudicator.
The other change I think is necessary in Canadian broadcasting is the extension of network facilities. As I have indicated, most programs still originate in urban areas. It should be noted that urban areas tend to be the source of the influences against which the Massey commission warned Canadians, these so-called American materialistic influences. So long as most of our programs originate in the big city studios of the C.B.C. we are going to be exposed to this dangerous materialism that is supposed to be of United States origin.
I know, of course, the difficulties of giving the small, local broadcasting stations access to the networks. They, perhaps, have not the same studio facilities. Still if we are really going to have a nationally representative broadcasting policy in Canada-and the minister in his statement last night emphasized that broadcasting has to take the national viewpoint-we must allow the local, private community stations easier access to the networks. The small station on the prairies, with its attempt to satisfy the cultural and entertainment demands of the area it is serving, is just as important to the total cultural picture in Canada as is the big C.B.C. studio operating in the populous and wealthy urban setting.
I have not made any direct reference to television in these remarks because while there is much in common there is also a degree of separation between the two media.
Special Committee on Broadcasting As television has developed during the past two and a half years it seems to me that it is paralleling the development of radio. Unfortunately it is moving into some of the same errors that radio committed in its earlier stage of development. The tendency in television has been toward complete monopoly of this important communication media whereas, as I have indicated, in radio we have been moving gradually away from complete monopoly and domination by the C.B.C.
I believe any argument we use for an independent regulatory body for radio has equal significance for T.V. broadcasting. There was some very interesting evidence of the indirect and subtle control that can be imposed upon private operators in this field in the last committee on broadcasting. The private broadcasters were making a very determined stand to do away with monopoly in telecasting at the very outset of television activities. But for some strange reason the resistance that had developed in the country prior to the meeting of the committee on broadcasting suddenly disappeared, and there was acquiescence in the government policy of monopoly. Perhaps it is only a coincidence that a good many of the private broadcasters at that time had applications for licences before the government. I say it might be only a coincidence, but it is also quite possible that they were afraid that if they defied government policy in reference to monopoly in telecasting they might run into difficulties in obtaining television channels.
That is merely one example of the subtle influence that can be exerted when the state medium of broadcasting and telecasting is both competitor and adjudicator. This unfortunate state of affairs would be completely removed if we had an independent regulatory body as they have in the federal communications commission in the United States, for example, supervising both these important activities in the broadcasting field.
There is another incident that comes to my mind as I consider this problem of a developing monopoly in T.V. Last evening the minister indicated that he felt a duplication of services in T.V. would weaken the strength and growing power of the national system as a whole. It is hard to see where competition between two stations in an area large enough to support a private station as well as a C.B.C. station would weaken the strength and growing power of the national system as a whole. I feel it would tend to strengthen the programming and general excellence of the activities of both. But applying this policy to its limits, of course, produces a ridiculous situation such as occurred in Hamilton, where the station has
1838	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Broadcasting been prohibited from telecasting in a direction that would interfere with the C.B.C. programming. In other words the government, instead of providing broader facilities and improving programs for the Canadian public, is deliberately narrowing the choice of Canadian citizens by subscribing to this monopoly program. Of course such a philosophy has very serious implications for a free society.
Television is just moving into network facilities. I was interested in hearing the minister's announcement that there will be microwave relay services available across Canada in the very near future. But, again, if we do not watch it, there is going to be a danger of concentration in urban areas. The monopoly position adopted by the C.B.C. up to the moment has meant that we And their operations restricted to the large, populous and wealthy urban communities. The smaller, less populous and less wealthy communities are privileged, if they behave themselves, to have private television operations.
I feel that if the private broadcasters were free of the continuing threat of competition and adjudication under a government controlled body, we would have more realistic ideas presented for the solution of these problems, and as a result we would move much more quickly to a telecasting program that would be truly representative of the national picture in Canada.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to reemphasize-
